explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “Stay here and keep watch.” He doesn't hand the three of them a big job. I think He wants them close and awake while He carries something heavy.

explanations.answer: Go back and get the others
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets sent off to round up anyone. Jesus has just told them His soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. His request is simple: “Stay here and keep watch.” Staying put sounds easy, and we'll see how that goes.

explanations.answer: Head into the city for help
explanations.explanation: No errands here, friend. Jesus doesn't send Peter, James and John anywhere. He asks them to stay with Him and keep watch. Sometimes the whole job is just being there.
Yes, He says it. After “Abba, Father,” Jesus says, “all things are possible for You.” Then He asks for the cup to be taken away. He's talking honestly to His Father about what's ahead.
The text says He does say it. Right after “Abba, Father,” Jesus says, “all things are possible for You.” It's the start of an honest prayer, and the ask comes right behind it.

explanations.answer: He wants the Father's will over His own
explanations.explanation: That's the heart of it. Jesus says, “Yet not what I will, but what You will.” The ask is real, and so is the yielding, both in one prayer. I think that's one of the most honest prayers in the whole Bible.

explanations.answer: He will wait until morning for an answer
explanations.explanation: Morning never comes up in His prayer. Right after asking for the cup to be taken, Jesus says, “Yet not what I will, but what You will.” He doesn't set a deadline for the Father. He hands the matter over.

explanations.answer: He will keep asking until it's taken away
explanations.explanation: That's not what He says. He does go back and pray again (Mark 14:39), but right after the ask, He says, “Yet not what I will, but what You will.” He puts the Father's will first, so He isn't pushing to get His way.

Sleeping it is. Peter, James and John, three of Jesus' disciples, were asked to keep watch and instead they're out cold. Jesus finds them that way and says, “Simon, are you asleep?” It's a very human moment, and I've been in the same spot with a long day and a warm blanket.
Jesus is the one praying here. When He returns, He finds Peter, James and John sleeping. That's why He asks, “Simon, are you asleep?”
They're not gone. Jesus comes back and finds Peter, James and John sleeping. Running off comes later in the passage, so hold on to that.

explanations.answer: So they won't enter into temptation
explanations.explanation: Right on target. Jesus says, “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.” Then He adds, “For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” He's looking out for them.

explanations.answer: So they can warn the other disciples
explanations.explanation: Warning others isn't what He says. Jesus gives the reason plainly: “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.” The watching is for their own sake.

explanations.answer: So His own prayer is answered sooner
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text ties their watching to His prayer being answered. Jesus says, “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.” The reason is about them, not about speeding anything up.

True, and it's a kind thing to say to sleepy friends. Jesus says, “For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” He says it right after telling them, “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.” He names it plainly.
It's true, and Jesus says it Himself. His words are, “For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” He says it after finding them sleeping.

Not this time, friend. Jesus goes away and prays again, and when He comes back, He finds them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. So they're not awake and keeping watch. Anybody who's ever tried to stay up past their limit knows how that goes.
Right, they're not awake. Jesus comes back a second time and finds them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. The watch isn't going well, and I think we've all had a night like that.

explanations.answer: They don't know what to answer
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Mark 14:40 says they did not know what to answer Him. I think when you've been caught napping on a job you were given, silence is the only thing you can come up with.
No promises are recorded here. The text says they did not know what to answer Him. I think when you've just been caught napping, a promise is a lot to come up with.
They don't offer that excuse. The text says they did not know what to answer Him. Nobody tries to explain it away.

explanations.answer: He is betrayed into the hands of sinners
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. Jesus tells them, “Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). The hour He prayed about has come.

explanations.answer: He is welcomed into the city by crowds
explanations.explanation: This is a very different scene from a welcome. Jesus says, “Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). Betrayal is what's coming, not a parade.

explanations.answer: He is called up to teach at the temple
explanations.explanation: Teaching isn't what He's talking about here. Jesus says, “Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). The hour has come, and it's a hard one.
Yes, His betrayer. Jesus says, “Rise, let us go. See, My betrayer is approaching!” He tells them to rise and then points out who is coming.
His mother isn't the one coming. Jesus says, “See, My betrayer is approaching!” Someone who has turned against Him is on the way.
That's not who Jesus names. He says, “See, My betrayer is approaching!” The one coming is the person who will hand Him over.
Swords and clubs, baker. The crowd with Judas, one of the Twelve, comes armed with exactly that. They were sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. Nobody brings clubs to a chat.

Spears and shields would look impressive, but the verse doesn't list them. What the crowd carries is swords and clubs. Judas arrives with them, and they were sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders.
Bows and arrows don't show up here. The text puts swords and clubs in the crowd's hands. The men who sent them were the chief priests, scribes, and elders.
That's the signal. Judas tells them, “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.” Then he goes directly to Jesus, says “Rabbi!” and kisses Him. A greeting turned into a sign.
Pointing isn't the plan. Judas tells them, “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.” The signal is a kiss.
Bowing isn't mentioned. The signal Judas arranges is a kiss: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.” That's how they'd know.
An outlaw, that's the word. Jesus asks, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw?” He sees what's happening and says it out loud.
A guest doesn't get swords and clubs, friend. Jesus asks, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw?” They're treating Him like an outlaw.

Teaching is what Jesus was doing, but it isn't what He says they're treating Him as. He asks, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw?” That's a very different way to treat Him.

True, baker. Jesus says, “Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me.” Every day, right out in the open. Then Judas shows up with a crowd armed with swords and clubs (Mark 14:43), and suddenly they're ready to arrest Him.
It's true, and Jesus says it Himself. His words are, “Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me.” He was out in the open and they didn't arrest Him.

explanations.answer: So the Scriptures would be fulfilled
explanations.explanation: That's the reason He gives. Jesus says, “But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” So what's unfolding here isn't random.

explanations.answer: Because Judas had a change of heart
explanations.explanation: Judas doesn't turn back in this passage. He kisses Jesus and the men seize Him. The reason Jesus gives is, “But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.”

explanations.answer: Because the crowd had grown afraid
explanations.explanation: The text never says the crowd was afraid. The reason Jesus gives is, “But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” He tells them straight out.
It's the opposite, friend. The text says, “Then everyone deserted Him and fled.” That's a heavy moment, so I think it's worth sitting with.
Right, they don't stay. The text says, “Then everyone deserted Him and fled.” I think this is one of the hardest lines in the passage.
He runs, baker. They caught hold of him, but he pulled free of the linen cloth and ran away naked. The cloth stayed behind and he kept going.
No fighting from him. They caught hold of the young man, but he pulled free of the linen cloth and ran away. He left with nothing but himself.
He doesn't give up, he gets out. They catch hold of him, but he pulls free of the linen cloth and runs away. Nothing in the text says he stuck around.
